\chapter{A Little, Enough, Quite a Lot}
\label{ch:mr-amounts}
\hlchaptermodality{54}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can measure out an amount of something on a four-step scale, stop somebody pouring, and exclaim how big or how beautiful a thing is.}

Complete MR-R54-how-much and run the amount scale, the degree scale and the exclamative in one pass -- thoDaM paaNii dyaa, khuup paaNii aahe, kitii lahaan!
\end{chapteropening}

\section[thoḍā]{\mr{थोडा} (thoḍā) — a little, some}

\label{lesson:MR-C54-thoda}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{जरा}} softens an adjective. It cannot measure out a quantity of something: \emph{jarā water} is not Marathi.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{jarā kaṭhīṇ}, then double a word to strengthen it
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{थोडा}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{थोडा}} — \emph{thoḍā} — \textbf{a little, some, a small amount of}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{थोडं} \mr{पाणी}} — \emph{thoḍaṁ pāṇī} — \textbf{a little water}
\end{quote}

The ending is where the difference lives. \textbf{\mr{थोडा}} ends in \textbf{-\mr{आ}}, so it \textbf{agrees}: \textbf{\mr{थोडा} \mr{चहा}} (masculine), \textbf{\mr{थोडं} \mr{पाणी}} (neuter). \textbf{\mr{जरा}} never changes. The two are close in meaning and behave in opposite ways, and the reason is that they are different parts of speech — \textbf{\mr{थोडा}} measures a NOUN, \textbf{\mr{जरा}} softens an adjective or a verb.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{थोडा} \mr{चहा}} — a little tea. \textbf{\mr{जरा} \mr{कठीण}} — slightly difficult.
\end{quote}

Its ancestor is Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{स्तोक}} (\emph{stoka}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a little, a drop},\textquotedblright{} worn down through the Prakrits. Hindi's \emph{thoṛā} is the same word by the same road.

Against \textbf{\mr{खूप}} it is the other end of the same scale: \textbf{\mr{खूप} \mr{पाणी}} is a lot of water, \textbf{\mr{थोडं} \mr{पाणी}} is a little.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{thoḍaṁ pāṇī}, \emph{thoḍā chahā} — and hear the ending move
  \item \emph{jarā} — and hear that it never would
  \item \emph{khūp pāṇī} against \emph{thoḍaṁ pāṇī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \textbf{\mr{थोडा}} and \textbf{\mr{जरा}} agrees, and why? (\textbf{\mr{थोडा}} — it measures a noun and ends in \textbf{-\mr{आ}}.) What Sanskrit word is it worn down from? (\textbf{\mr{स्तोक}}, a drop.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A5\%E0\%A5\%8B\%E0\%A4\%A1\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{थोडा}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[puresā]{\mr{पुरेसा} (puresā) — enough}

\label{lesson:MR-C54-puresa}



\begin{quote}
A little and a lot are both amounts. Neither one says the amount is right.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{पुरेसा}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{पुरेसा}} — \emph{puresā} — \textbf{enough, sufficient}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{पुरेसं} \mr{पाणी}} — \emph{puresaṁ pāṇī} — \textbf{enough water}
\end{quote}

Another \textbf{-\mr{आ}} word, so it agrees and you already have all three forms: \textbf{\mr{पुरेसा} \mr{चहा}}, \textbf{\mr{पुरेसं} \mr{पाणी}}.

Said on its own it closes a transaction. \textbf{\mr{पुरे}!} is \emph{that's enough}, and a Marathi host pouring tea will stop when you say it — which is a more useful thing to own than it sounds, because the alternative is \textbf{\mr{नको}}, and \textbf{\mr{नको}} refuses the whole offer rather than the next spoonful.

That \textbf{\mr{पुरे}} is the word underneath \textbf{\mr{पुरेसा}}, and it comes from the Sanskrit root \textbf{\mr{पूर्}} (\emph{pūr-}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to fill}.\textquotedblright{} Enough is \emph{filled}. The same ancient root gives Latin \emph{plenus} and English \textbf{full}, so the idea has travelled a long way without changing.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{puresaṁ pāṇī}, \emph{puresā chahā}
  \item \emph{pure!} — that's enough
  \item \emph{thoḍaṁ}, \emph{puresaṁ}, \emph{khūp} — three amounts, smallest first
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\mr{पुरे}} stop, and what does \textbf{\mr{नको}} stop? (\textbf{\mr{पुरे}} stops the pouring; \textbf{\mr{नको}} refuses the offer.) What does the root \textbf{\mr{पूर्}} mean? (\textbf{To fill}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AA\%E0\%A5\%81\%E0\%A4\%B0\%E0\%A5\%87\%E0\%A4\%B8\%E0\%A4\%BE}{Wiktionary: \mr{पुरेसा}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[barāch]{\mr{बराच} (barāch) — quite a lot}

\label{lesson:MR-C54-barach}



\begin{quote}
A little, enough, a lot. There is a step between \emph{enough} and \emph{a lot} that Marathi bothers to name.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{बराच}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{बराच}} — \emph{barāch} — \textbf{quite a lot, a fair amount, rather}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{बरंच} \mr{पाणी}} — \emph{baraṁch pāṇī} — \textbf{quite a lot of water}
\end{quote}

You already own both halves of this word. \textbf{\mr{बरा}} is the \emph{fine, all right} of chapter four — the \textbf{\mr{बरं}} you answer \emph{how are you} with — and \textbf{-\mr{च}} is Marathi's little emphatic tail, the one that means \emph{precisely that}. Glue them together and \emph{a fair amount} is literally \emph{a good-ish bit}.

It agrees, because the \textbf{\mr{बरा}} underneath it ends in \textbf{-\mr{आ}}: \textbf{\mr{बराच} \mr{चहा}}, \textbf{\mr{बरंच} \mr{पाणी}}.

Set the four amounts in order and the scale is complete:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{थोडं}} a little · \textbf{\mr{पुरेसं}} enough · \textbf{\mr{बरंच}} quite a lot · \textbf{\mr{खूप}} a lot.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{baraṁch pāṇī} — quite a lot of water
  \item which taught word is hiding inside it — \emph{\textbf{\mr{बरा}}}
  \item the four amounts in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two pieces is \textbf{\mr{बराच}} made of? (\emph{\textbf{\mr{बरा}}} and the emphatic \emph{\textbf{-\mr{च}}}.) Which of the four amount words does NOT agree? (\textbf{\mr{खूप}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AC\%E0\%A4\%B0\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%9A}{Wiktionary: \mr{बराच}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kitī moṭhaṁ!]{\mr{किती} \mr{मोठं}! (kitī moṭhaṁ!) — how big!}

\label{lesson:MR-C54-kiti-excl}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{किती}} has asked for a number since chapter thirty-seven. Put it in front of an adjective instead of a noun and it stops asking.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{किती} with an adjective}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{किती} \mr{मोठं}!} — \emph{kitī moṭhaṁ!} — \textbf{how big!}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{किती} \mr{सुंदर}!} — \emph{kitī sundar!} — \textbf{how beautiful!}
\end{quote}

Same word, different neighbour, different job. In front of a \textbf{noun} — \textbf{\mr{किती} \mr{भाऊ}?} — \textbf{\mr{किती}} asks for a number. In front of an \textbf{adjective} it exclaims, and no number is wanted or given.

Two things tell the listener which one you mean. On the page it is the \textbf{!} you learned in chapter thirty-three, where a question would have carried \textbf{?}. Out loud it is the tune: the exclamation \textbf{falls} at the end where a question \textbf{rises}. Say the pair back to back and hear your own voice do it.

English works exactly this way — \emph{how many?} against \emph{how lovely!} — so this is a construction you can feel rather than one you have to install.

The adjective still agrees, and there is nothing else to remember: \textbf{\mr{किती} \mr{मोठं}!} of a house, \textbf{\mr{किती} \mr{मोठी}!} of a room.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kitī sundar!} — and let the voice fall
  \item \emph{kitī bhāū?} — and let it rise
  \item \emph{kitī moṭhaṁ!} of a house, then \emph{kitī moṭhī!} of a room
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What decides whether \textbf{\mr{किती}} asks or exclaims? (\textbf{Whether a noun or an adjective follows it}.) Which mark ends the exclamation, and what does the voice do? (\textbf{!}; \textbf{it falls}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[thoḍaṁ · puresaṁ · baraṁch · khūp]{How much, how strong, and how!}

\label{lesson:MR-R54-how-much}



\begin{quote}
Two chapters, seven items, and not one of them was an adjective. Name the four amounts in order before you use any of them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{thoḍaṁ · puresaṁ · baraṁch · khūp} — the amounts, smallest first
  \item \emph{jarā · khūp · khūp khūp} — the degrees, quietest first
  \item \emph{kitī lahān!} — and let the voice fall on the \textbf{!}
  \item \emph{kitī?} — and let it rise on the \textbf{?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the four amount words never changes its ending? (\textbf{\mr{खूप}}.) What turns \textbf{\mr{किती}} from a question into an exclamation? (\textbf{An adjective after it instead of a noun}.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
